nature-eco-084.title: Bushmeat: wild meat, food security and vanishing species
nature-eco-084.text: As of 2016, 301 land mammal species were threatened with extinction by bushmeat hunting, including every species of pangolin. Bushmeat is meat from wild animals hunted for people to eat, especially in Africa. For poor rural communities in the humid forests of the tropics, it is a main source of animal protein and income. The trade in West and Central Africa was estimated at 1–5 million tonnes a year around the turn of the 21st century. Hunting for a family's own use in large landscapes can be sustainable. Market hunting is another matter. It threatens large, slow-breeding species, a clear case of {{ref:nature-eco-063}}. Logging roads and trucks give hunters access to remote forests and carry the meat to towns. The phrase "bushmeat crisis", coined in 2007, names the double threat of vanishing food supplies and wildlife extinctions. Suggested remedies include affordable alternative protein, giving communities rights over wildlife, and enforcing the protection of reserves.

nature-eco-056.title: Why forests are over-cleared: the benefits no one pays for
nature-eco-056.text: A forest's timber has a price, but many of its other benefits do not. Many important forest functions have no markets, and hence no economic value readily apparent to forest owners or the communities that depend on them. This gap, a case of {{ref:nature-econ-177}}, is the economic reason forests are over-cleared. Owners see more profit in converting a forest than in keeping it. Yet short-term gains from converting forest or overharvesting wood typically cost long-term income and biological productivity. Studies found poverty and agricultural rent, the income land earns from farming, to be principal factors behind deforestation. Proposed policies would align economic activity in critical forests with their value for ecosystem services and climate mitigation. Their tools include certification, traceability, which tracks where products come from, and the trade charges described in {{ref:nature-pol-112}}.

nature-eco-126.title: Habitat conservation: protecting the places species live
nature-eco-126.text: Repairing a damaged ecosystem is thought to cost far more than conserving it in the first place. Habitat conservation is the management of habitats to protect and restore them, and to stop species from going extinct, being fragmented or losing range. It is a central practice of {{ref:nature-eco-140}}. Natural habitats provide ecosystem services, such as timber from forests and clean water from streams. Conserving them can also pay through tourism and time spent outdoors. Putting a value on conserving different areas is often criticized as too utilitarian, judging nature only by its usefulness. Priority usually goes to {{ref:nature-eco-081}} and to the homes of flagship, umbrella or at-risk species. Crops show what is at stake. Wild relatives of crops resist disease better, and the wild corn teosinte resists 4 corn diseases. Seed banks plus habitat conservation are therefore proposed to secure food supplies. Scientific uncertainty is handled by the approach described in {{ref:nature-nbs-146}}, which gathers information and adjusts conservation plans over time.

nature-eco-130.title: Indirect drivers: the forces behind the bulldozer
nature-eco-130.text: A bulldozer clearing forest is the visible end of a long chain. Indirect drivers are the political, economic and social forces that give rise to the human activities that harm the environment. They include population, economic development, urbanization, technology and climate change. Direct drivers, such as mining, agriculture, urban infrastructure and transport, result from them. Together they shape {{ref:nature-eco-129}}. Consumption beyond what ecosystems can sustain can be measured with the tool described in {{ref:nature-acct-027}}. Impact depends on lifestyle, affluence and pollution as much as on the raw number of people. Cultural values matter too: how a society views nature shapes how hard it works to preserve it. Blaming growing human numbers for environmental problems is controversial. Critics say it can unfairly blame poor people in the Global South.

nature-eco-036.title: HIPPO and the Evil Quartet: naming the drivers of loss
nature-eco-036.text: Edward O. Wilson boiled the problem down to one acronym, HIPPO: Habitat destruction, Invasive species, Pollution, human over-Population and Over-harvesting. Jared Diamond's version is an "Evil Quartet" of habitat destruction, overkill, introduced species and secondary extinctions. Both lists name the main human pressures behind {{ref:nature-eco-035}}. Today's fuller list is habitat loss, land-use intensification, pollution, overexploitation, invasive species and climate change. Habitat destruction leads worldwide. At sea, a 2019 report by the panel described in {{ref:nature-gov-020}} found catching too many fish to be the main driver of mass extinction. Invasive species can drive natives extinct by outcompeting them, pushing them out of their role in the ecosystem, or interbreeding with them. The pressures also interact. In 2021 the same panel and the UN's climate science panel issued a joint report. It found that biodiversity loss and climate change must be tackled together, because they are inextricably linked.

nature-eco-037.title: Farming, the largest driver of biodiversity loss on land
nature-eco-037.text: As of 2023, about 38% of Earth's land surface was used for agriculture, the dominant use of land. That reach makes farming the largest single cause of biodiversity decline on land. As farmland expands and intensifies, it converts and degrades natural habitat, the process described in {{ref:nature-eco-041}}. The 2019 global assessment described in {{ref:nature-eco-123}} found industrial agriculture to be the primary driver of biodiversity collapse. A 2014 UN outlook report estimated that agriculture causes 70% of projected biodiversity loss on land. Animal farming takes the biggest share of space. Livestock systems occupy about 77% of agricultural land but provide less than 20% of the world's calories. The pressure is set to grow. More than 17,000 species risk losing habitat by 2050 as farming expands to meet food needs. Diet is one lever. A global shift toward mostly plant-based diets would free land for restoring ecosystems and biodiversity.

nature-eco-027.title: The $423 billion bill for invasive species
nature-eco-027.text: The economic impact of invasive species was estimated to exceed $423 billion a year as of 2019. That cost has quadrupled every decade since 1970. It covers the money lost to damage from invasive species and the money spent on controlling them, a form of {{ref:nature-econ-114}}. The costs split into direct production losses in farming and forestry and the costs of management. In the United States, estimated damage and control costs exceed $138 billion a year. In France, damage costs were nearly eight times higher than spending on management. Even these figures understate the bill. Valuing lost species and ecosystem services would raise it sharply. Some invaders bring benefits, such as invasive trees used in commercial forestry, but their returns are usually far smaller than their costs. Early detection and rapid response is often called the key to management. It helps only when reintroduction is rare and response is affordable.

nature-eco-154.title: Wildlife trade: a vast, poorly watched market
nature-eco-154.text: Global imports of wildlife products were worth US$187 billion in 2012, with fish and other catches from the sea and fresh water making up $113 billion. Wildlife trade is the exchange of products from wild animals or plants, taken from nature or raised in captivity, whether alive, dead or as parts. Legal trade is regulated by the agreement described in {{ref:nature-mkt-001}}, which has 184 member countries, called Parties. Illegal trade is one of the major illegal economic activities, comparable to drug and arms trafficking. Interpol puts it at $10 billion to $20 billion a year. Trade and other use are the second major threat to endangered mammals, and among the top ten threats to birds, amphibians and cycads. Live wildlife markets have been linked to outbreaks of diseases including COVID-19, H5N1 bird flu, SARS and mpox. The trade is poorly monitored, because customs codes record most wildlife imports only under broad categories. Legal trade can also help. Quotas on Florida alligators give an economic incentive to keep habitat.

nature-eco-134.title: Island biogeography: why small, remote places hold fewer species
nature-eco-134.text: Simberloff and Wilson once cleared every arthropod, the group of jointed-legged animals that includes insects, from small Florida islands of salt-tolerant trees, the coastal forests described in {{ref:nature-eco-410}}. Within a year the islands were recolonized, nearer islands fastest. Island biogeography studies what controls the number of species and how they diversify in isolated natural communities. Robert MacArthur and E. O. Wilson started the field in the 1960s. Its theory holds that an island's species count is set by a balance between new arrivals and extinction. Remote islands receive fewer immigrants. Larger islands have more habitat and a lower chance of species dying out by bad luck. An 'island' can be any patch of suitable habitat surrounded by unsuitable land, such as a mountaintop, a woodland or a park amid development. Seeing reserves as habitat islands raised fears that they would lose species. That fear led to wildlife corridors and to a vigorous debate over how reserves should be laid out, the subject of {{ref:nature-mkt-009}}.

nature-eco-050.title: Defaunation: the quiet emptying of animal life
nature-eco-050.text: More than 50 percent of all wildlife is estimated to have been lost in the last 40 years. Defaunation is the global, local or functional loss of animal populations or species from ecological communities. Unlike extinction, it counts falling animal numbers as well as disappearing species. Growing human numbers and better harvesting technology have stripped large vertebrates from many communities. Large mammals are especially vulnerable because they need large home ranges. Invasive species matter too: over 50% of extinct animal species with a known cause were affected by them. Tropical regions such as the Brazilian Amazon, the Congo Basin and Indonesia are hit hardest. The losses are old as well as new. Links in the food webs of land mammals have fallen by 53% over the past 130,000 years as humans expanded. Emptier communities work less well. Defaunation can weaken services such as nutrient cycling, decomposition, pollinating crops, controlling pests and keeping water clean.

nature-eco-087.title: Conservation status: rating a species' risk of extinction
nature-eco-087.text: Counting the animals left is not enough to judge a species' danger. Conservation status is a rating of whether a species or other group still exists and how likely it is to go extinct in the near future. Assessments weigh population trends, breeding success and known threats, not just how many individuals remain. Two international systems exist, run by the IUCN and by the trade agreement described in {{ref:nature-mkt-001}}. Others work at regional, national and local levels. The best known is the IUCN's list described in {{ref:nature-acct-076}}. It sorts species into nine groups using criteria such as rate of decline, population size, range and fragmentation. Three categories, critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable, together count as "threatened". The rest run from Extinct and Extinct in the Wild to Near Threatened, Least Concern and Data Deficient. The trade agreement, in force since 1975, aims to ensure that trade between countries in wild animals and plants does not threaten their survival. Guides that help shoppers choose seafood rate species in a similar way. They also weigh fishing harms such as catching unwanted animals by accident and dragging heavy nets along the seabed.

nature-eco-099.title: Endangered species and the bald eagle's comeback
nature-eco-099.text: In 1963 the United States had just 417 nesting pairs of bald eagles. By 2020 it had 71,400, thanks to habitat protection, legal protection and a ban on the pesticide DDT. An endangered species is one at very high risk of going extinct in the near future, worldwide or in a particular region. On the IUCN's Red List, described in {{ref:nature-eco-087}}, "Endangered" sits between "Vulnerable" and "Critically Endangered". The criteria are specific. One is a population that falls 20% within five years and has fewer than 2,500 mature individuals left. Another is a decline of 50% to 70% over 10 years or three generations, whichever is longer. Species become endangered mainly through habitat loss and loss of genetic variation. In 2026 the Red List named 49,500 species worldwide as threatened with extinction. Many nations respond by banning hunting or harvest, restricting development or setting land aside as reserves.

nature-eco-151.title: Threatened species: the red-listed 40 percent
nature-eco-151.text: About 40% of the 40,177 species assessed under the IUCN's Red List criteria are listed as threatened, a total of 16,119. A threatened species is any animal, plant or fungus species vulnerable to extinction in the near future. The IUCN, the foremost authority, groups three categories as threatened: critically endangered, endangered and vulnerable, as {{ref:nature-eco-087}} explains. Near threatened, least concern, not evaluated and data deficient species are not counted. Threatened species are also called red-listed species, after the IUCN's Red List of Threatened Species. The label reaches below whole species, too. Subspecies, populations and stocks can also be classed as threatened.

nature-eco-078.title: The background extinction rate: nature's normal pace
nature-eco-078.text: At nature's normal pace, one bird species would go extinct about every 400 years. The background extinction rate is the normal rate at which species go extinct through Earth's history, outside mass extinctions. It is roughly one extinction per million species-years. In other words, among a million species watched for a year, about one would vanish. Extinction is a normal part of evolution, and the background rate measures how often it happens naturally. At normal rates species typically last 5–10 million years, and mammal species about 1 million years on average. The rate is not fixed. It has fallen over the Phanerozoic, the current eon of abundant animal life, a decline linked to rising oxygen in the oceans. Its main use is as a yardstick, showing how much faster species are vanishing today.

nature-eco-112.title: Mass extinctions: when life's variety collapses
nature-eco-112.text: The end-Permian 'Great Dying' killed about 81% of marine species and an estimated 70% of land vertebrate species. It was the largest extinction event, or mass extinction: a widespread and rapid fall in the variety of life on Earth. Such events happen when extinctions outpace both the normal {{ref:nature-eco-078}} and the rate at which new species form. Estimates of how many major ones occurred in the last 540 million years range from five to more than twenty. Large extinctions tend to follow when a biosphere already under long-term stress suffers a short-term shock. Scientists still debate the causes of each one. Afterward, usually only adaptable 'weedy' species survive, and new groups can take over the emptied niches. Research since 1982 concludes that a sixth mass extinction caused by human activity is under way, with extinctions over 1,000 times the background rate since 1900. It is driven by growing populations, economic growth and the overuse of nature's resources.

nature-eco-022.title: The Holocene extinction: the sixth great dying, caused by people
nature-eco-022.text: Species are now disappearing an estimated 100 to 1,000 times faster than the natural background rate. The Holocene extinction is this ongoing wave of extinctions of plants and animals, on land and at sea, caused by human activity in the current geological epoch. It is sometimes called the sixth extinction, after the five earlier mass extinctions described in {{ref:nature-eco-112}}. When the emphasis falls on human causes, it is also called the Anthropocene extinction. A 2023 study counted at least 73 animal genera, groups of closely related species, lost since 1500. It judged that rate 35 times higher than the background rate without human impacts. The 2019 assessment described in {{ref:nature-eco-123}} estimated that about one million species are at risk of extinction within decades because of human activities. The drivers include climate change, deforestation, the destruction of swamps and marshes, fishing too hard, ocean acidification, growing populations, economic growth and rising consumption, especially in affluent societies. Scientists broadly agree that habitat destruction, resource consumption and the elimination of species are the main human drivers. Beneath them lie two centuries of growth in population, in economic output and in consumption per person. Proposed remedies include shifting economic activity toward low-impact sectors, plant-based diets, and enlarging the areas protected on land and at sea.

nature-eco-110.title: Extinction debt: species doomed by losses already made
nature-eco-110.text: In the Azores, over 95% of native forest was destroyed in 600 years. More than half of the islands' arthropods are now thought committed to extinction, still alive but doomed. That is extinction debt: the future extinction of species already set in motion by past events such as habitat loss. It arises from time lags. Long-lived trees, for example, may survive for years after new trees can no longer be produced. Habitat fragmentation and habitat destruction are its best-known drivers, because they cut off species' ability to recolonize other patches. The debt is most likely in long-lived species and in specialists with narrow habitat needs. Tilman, May, Lehman and Nowak first used the term in 1994. It is likened to the 'climate commitment' of warming that continues after emissions stop. Modeling suggests that 80–90% of the extinctions due to past Amazon deforestation have yet to happen. Protecting today's habitat may not be enough. Still, the long delay gives time for restoration to prevent losses.

nature-eco-157.title: How climate change spreads infectious disease
nature-eco-157.text: Dengue and Lyme disease now appear at higher latitudes and elevations than before. Warmer, wetter conditions let the mosquitoes and ticks that carry such diseases survive in places once too cold or dry. Climate change is altering how widely and heavily many infectious diseases are transmitted around the world. Warmer water and more flooding spread bacteria such as Vibrio cholerae. Drought and poor water access raise the risk of diarrheal diseases. Damage to nature adds to the danger. Deforestation, habitat fragmentation and biodiversity loss raise the risk of diseases jumping from animals to people, as people encroach on habitats and ecosystems favor efficient disease carriers. Low-income communities with weak healthcare and sanitation are the most vulnerable. Diseases like malaria slow their path to prosperity, worsening global inequality. The UN Environment Programme says the most fundamental protection against diseases from animals is to prevent the destruction of nature. Responses increasingly follow the One Health approach, which treats human, animal and environmental health as one.

nature-eco-146.title: Soil biodiversity: the hidden life beneath a football pitch
nature-eco-146.text: A football pitch is estimated to hold underground organisms equal in mass to 500 sheep. Soil biodiversity is the variety of life in soil, along with the soil properties that can be managed to support it. Soil is home mainly to microbes such as bacteria and fungi, but also to protozoa, nematodes, microarthropods, earthworms, termites and millipedes. Their main job is breaking down and reusing organic matter from the plant-based food web above ground. Keeping soil fertile has been called one of the most vital ecological services the living world performs. Microbial secretions do most of the work of binding soil particles into crumbs, called aggregates, and they protect soil carbon from breakdown. Erosion, acidification, salinization and chloride from potash fertilizer all threaten soil organisms. Because soils are a dispersed asset, healthy soil is best secured by a broad, consistent and economically appealing approach. Liming is one example, and the plow-free method described in {{ref:nature-nbs-290}} is another.

nature-eco-131.title: In-situ conservation: saving species where they live
nature-eco-131.text: Moving a species elsewhere is the fallback; keeping it at home comes first. In-situ conservation protects species and their genetic material on site, in the natural populations where they live. Its methods include nature reserves, parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biodiversity hotspots and gene sanctuaries. Keeping populations in the setting where they developed their traits lets evolution and adaptation carry on. Reserves must be large enough to hold populations with the genetic diversity needed to keep adapting. The opposite approach, {{ref:nature-eco-074}}, keeps threatened species or their material elsewhere, as in seed libraries and gene banks. It is a last resort when in situ conservation is too difficult or impossible.

nature-eco-114.title: Climate change as a threat of extinction
nature-eco-114.text: Today 84% of coral-built reefs could withstand marine heatwaves. At 1.5 °C of warming, 2022 estimates suggest, only 0.2% could. Climate change can drive species extinct by pushing temperature and weather outside the conditions each evolved to live in, its niche. A species can adapt where it is or move. So far the IUCN links only 20 of 864 recorded species extinctions to climate, usually on weak evidence. Projections are grimmer. A 2011 review of 74 studies found an average projected loss of 11.2% of species by 2100. For insects, a 2018 study looked at three levels of warming: 1.5 °C, 2 °C and 3.2 °C. It estimated that 6%, 18% and about 49% of species, respectively, would lose over half their climatic range. A 2021 estimate that warming like that of the Big Five would bring a similar mass extinction was disputed the next year. At sea, climate already threatens 45% of at-risk species, though fishing and pollution do more damage for now. Prevention means limiting warming and protecting habitat, as in the 30x30 effort.

nature-eco-124.title: Global biodiversity: how many species share the Earth
nature-eco-124.text: About 1.74 million species had been catalogued by 2018, yet over 80% of species have not been described at all. Global biodiversity is the total variety of life forms on Earth. Nobody knows its size. Estimates of the number of species alive today run from 2 million to 1 trillion. Most are around 11 million or fewer, and the highest figures are disputed. Insects dominate, with about 1,000,000 described and an estimated 5,000,000 in all. The total rises as new species form and falls with extinction, at a background rate of about one extinction per million species-years. Habitat destruction, often to expand farming, is currently a bigger driver of loss than climate change. The world has struggled to slow it. Of 20 global targets set in 2010, described in {{ref:nature-gov-017}}, only six were 'partially achieved' by 2020.

nature-eco-156.title: Forest genetic resources: the variety inside trees
nature-eco-156.text: In 2014 the FAO's first State of the World's Forest Genetic Resources found half the regularly used forest species threatened by land conversion, overexploitation and climate change. Forest genetic resources are the genetic material, of present or future value, of forest tree and shrub species. Forest communities depend on them for timber and for products such as fruits, gums and resins, and they underpin plantation wood. Their diversity lets tree species adapt to climate change. Not all can adapt fast enough, so moving seed and other forest reproductive material may be needed.

nature-eco-054.title: Gross loss versus net change in forest area
nature-eco-054.text: A country can lose forest every year and still gain forest overall. The difference lies between gross forest loss and net change, which subtracts new forest gained from forest lost over a period. Deforestation is the conversion of forest to other uses, whether or not people caused it. Net change can be positive or negative, depending on whether gains exceed losses. Replanting and new planting, especially in East Asia, are increasing forest area, which grew in 22 of the 50 most forested nations.

nature-eco-057.title: Indigenous land rights as a brake on deforestation
nature-eco-057.text: In Brazil, forests held under Indigenous tenure are cleared at even lower rates than government parks. Handing legal rights over forest land to the Indigenous people and communities who live there is one way to slow deforestation, an application of {{ref:nature-econ-621}}. Supporters argue that moving land from public ownership to Indigenous inhabitants is a cost-effective way to conserve forests. Community concessions in Congolian rainforests show much less deforestation, because communities have reason to manage their land sustainably.

nature-eco-059.title: Rainforests are not the planet's oxygen supply
nature-eco-059.text: Many people believe rainforests supply much of the world's oxygen. They do not. Rainforests add little net oxygen to the atmosphere, so deforestation barely changes oxygen levels. About 50 percent of Earth's oxygen is produced by algae, mostly in the oceans. The case against clearing forests rests on other harms, set out in {{ref:nature-eco-053}}.
